A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same survey, with readable main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and Appendix A. Corresponding content can be matched despite relocation, renumbering, and expansion.

before.justification: v1 summarizes findings from cited studies, including its appendix tables. It reports no original experimental or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: Section 7.2 and footnote 10 report the authors' analysis of six models' VoiceBench and MMAU scores, finding a negative correlation. This constitutes original analysis of existing results. The added latency table separately compiles results attributed to other sources.

M1.justification: The encoder–adapter–sequence model–decoder formulation and three SLM categories remain unchanged. Newly discussed models and tokenization approaches expand the literature survey rather than modify a method proposed by this work.

E1.justification: v1 describes VoiceBench and MMAU as existing benchmarks; v2 additionally uses their scores in its own six-model analysis. This adds limited empirical coverage of content-focused question answering and broader audio understanding. Other newly surveyed benchmarks are not established as evaluations performed by this work.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates a proposed method against an experimental baseline suite. The expanded model catalog, cited cascade comparisons, and literature-sourced latency table do not establish additions to such a baseline suite.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a comparison of six models using VoiceBench overall scores and MMAU average test scores, specifying MMAU-v05.15.25 and an October 3, 2025 comparison date. v1 has no corresponding analysis protocol. The PDFs do not establish fresh benchmark inference runs.

E4.justification: The new VoiceBench–MMAU analysis examines whether the same models perform similarly across two benchmarks. This is a limited supplementary consistency analysis beyond v1's benchmark descriptions, rather than a new model ablation or robustness experiment.

E5.justification: v2 introduces correlation estimation across six models, reporting only the coefficient's negative sign. v1 contains no corresponding statistical analysis. The coefficient type and value, confidence interval, significance test, and repeated-run information are not supplied.

E6.justification: v2 adds the negative benchmark-correlation finding and Table 3's sourced latency results. For example, GLM-4-Voice is reported at 3244 ms on A40 and 1563 ms on L40 in different cited evaluations. These are newly reported results, not a comparable before-and-after performance gain.

T1.justification: The architectural definitions, autoregressive assumptions, and Q-Former attention expression remain substantively unchanged. Equation numbering, matrix orientation conventions, variable names, and the corrected text-output label are notation edits, not new mathematical reasoning or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contribution: a unifying survey organized around SLM architectures, training, evaluation, and challenges toward universal speech processing. The expanded coverage and supporting analysis do not redefine that contribution.

C2.justification: Section 7 adds substantial interpretation of disagreements between linguistic and acoustic benchmarks, cascade versus end-to-end trade-offs, and limitations of conversational evaluation. New discussion connects semantic performance, paralinguistics, latency, catastrophic forgetting, and human interaction quality. Section 8 also adds the need for latency and turn-taking benchmarking.

D1.justification: Footnote 10 supplies source locations and a benchmark version for the new analysis. Table 3 documents model sizes and hardware, while Appendix Tables 4–5 add technical descriptions, including Qwen2-Audio's 500k training hours. These are added disclosures, not evidence that existing experiments changed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the surveyed literature across tokenization, continuous speech modeling, alignment, reasoning, and conversational evaluation. Examples include PAST, Flow-SLM, CALM, OpusLM, Full-Duplex-Bench, and StressTest. It also develops the relationship to earlier cascaded systems and newer surveys; publication-metadata updates alone are not counted.

P1.justification: The eight-section organization and most existing prose remain. v2 copyedits terminology and grammar, clarifies architectural and metric explanations, adds evaluation subheadings, and introduces interactivity as a fourth evaluation category. Reorganization is localized rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The expanded timeline moves from Appendix Figure 6 to main-text Figure 1. The model catalog is redesigned from v1 Table 3 into v2 Tables 4–5 with descriptive columns and shaded rows, and a new latency table is added. The five architectural diagrams are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v1 discusses duplex architectures without a corresponding interactivity-evaluation category; v2 supplies that connection and clearer cascade/end-to-end trade-offs. The descriptive model catalog also improves navigation. These provide useful gains, although the new six-model correlation lacks model identities, individual scores, and coefficient details, limiting its reproducibility and evidentiary value.
